metrics.label: Front-foot contact to release

metrics.label: Elbow extension (UAH → release)
metrics.note: Elbow extension needs a side-on clip at 120–240 fps; it isn't estimated from this video. Never a substitute for an accredited ICC test.
metrics.norm: Legal bowlers: 0-10° (mean ~6°); ICC limit 15°

metrics.label: Front knee at release

metrics.label: Front knee bend after landing
metrics.note: Not measurable from this camera view — film side-on to measure it.

metrics.label: Back knee at back-foot contact
metrics.note: Not measurable from this camera view — film side-on to measure it.
metrics.norm: Injured bowlers 146° vs uninjured 156° at BFC (rear hip/knee)

priorities.headline: High side-bend at release (50°)
priorities.evidence: Moderate evidence in juniors, contested in adults
priorities.why: Lateral flexion of the trunk away from the bowling arm. Large side-bend loads the lower back; it is one of the better single-camera measures from behind the bowler.

drill.title: Stay tall at release
drill.cue: Head over the front foot, front arm drives towards the target rather than yanking down.
drills: Chalk-line run-ups: run and land on a straight line so the body isn't forced to lean (3 × 6).
Front-arm drive drill: hand reaches towards the target and finishes near the chest (2 × 10).
Wall drill: bowl alongside a wall/net on the non-bowling side to discourage falling away (2 × 8).

priorities.headline: Release point is low (85% of height)
priorities.why: Height of the ball at release as a percentage of your height (~1.53 m for a stature of 1.80 m). Single-camera precision is about ± 8 points.

drill.title: Get taller at release
drill.cue: Stand tall on your front leg and let the ball go at the top of your natural arm path.
drills: High-target drill: release over a raised rope/bar 1 m in front of the crease (3 × 6).
Standing-start bowling focusing on reaching up through the bowling arm (3 × 6).

priorities.headline: Slow from front-foot contact to release (333 ms)
priorities.why: How quickly you go from landing to letting the ball go. Shorter (with a stable front leg) usually means better energy transfer.

drill.title: Quicker through the crease
drill.cue: Land and go — front foot down, arm over, no pause.
drills: Short run-up (5 steps) focusing on the time from front-foot landing to release (3 × 6).
Metronome / clap timing: the release follows the front-foot 'thud' immediately (2 × 8).

advice: Show this to a coach and work on the drills in your practice plan.
Lower-back stress injuries are most common in teenage fast bowlers, especially in the two to three years after a growth spurt. Stick to the bowling limits in your plan.
If you get lower back pain while bowling (or any pain that changes how you bowl or lasts to the next day), stop and see a sports doctor or physiotherapist before bowling again.

notes: Bowling limits for 13–14 bowlers (Cricket Australia junior pace bowling guidelines): at most 5 overs per spell and 12 overs (72 deliveries) per day, up to 3 bowling days a week. At least one day off after every bowling day. Take at least 20 minutes between spells at training. Every delivery counts, including warm-up and drill balls: each session in the plan is counted and stays well inside the limit. Warm-up and drill balls are bowled in short sets with breaks; only the spell is bowled straight through.
Coming back after a break? Build up over about 4 weeks before bowling flat out.

In a long net session, bowl for no more than about 30 minutes at a stretch, then rest for as long. Plan a lighter week every 4–6 weeks, and after a growth spurt bowl shorter spells or less often for a while.
Stop bowling and see a physio or sports doctor if you get lower back pain, or any pain that changes how you bowl or is still there the next day.

fixes.title: Stay tall at release
fixes.why: Leaning sideways at release loads one side of the lower back and tends to drag the ball off line.
fixes.cue: Head over the front foot, front arm drives towards the target rather than yanking down.

fixes.title: Get taller at release
fixes.what: Release point is low (85% of height)
fixes.why: A higher release point makes the most of your height and gives the ball more bounce.
fixes.cue: Stand tall on your front leg and let the ball go at the top of your natural arm path.
